Adam is the name given in Genesis 1-5 to the first human.

Alexandra Kollontai was Soviet politician and diplomat (1872–1952).

Annalena Baerbock (born 15 December 1980) is a German diplomat and politician of the Alliance 90/The Greens party.
This 9th-century Iranian revolutionary's uprising was considered an offshoot of neo-Mazdakism and showed the enduring strength of pre-Islamic Persian identity in the region — who led it?

Babak Khorramdin (795 or 798 - January 838) was one of the main Iranian revolutionary leaders of the Iranian Khorram-Dinn ("Those of the joyous religion"), which was a local freedom movement fighting the Abbasid Caliphate.
Which former campaign manager for Hillary Clinton represented Brooklyn on the City Council before being elected mayor of New York City in 2013?
Bill de Blasio (born Warren Wilhelm Jr., May 8, 1961) is an American former politician who served as the 110th mayor of New York City from 2014 to 2021.
Having founded Turkey's first bank, İş Bankası, this politician went on to become prime minister under Atatürk and later the country's president throughout the 1950s — who is he?
Celâl Bayar (16 May 1883 - 22 August 1986) was a Turkish economist and politician who was the president of Turkey from 1950 to 1960.

This 8th-century Byzantine emperor exploited civil war in the Muslim world to press the Arab frontier, then resettled Christians in Thrace to tighten his grip on the Balkans against the Bulgars — who was he?
Constantine V (July 718 - 14 September 775) was Byzantine emperor from 741 to 775.

Dick Cheney (January 30, 1941 - November 3, 2025) was an American politician and businessman who served as the 46th vice president of the United States under President George W. Bush.
A daughter of Peter the Great, she ruled from 1741 to 1762 and stayed beloved partly for a remarkable vow: not to execute a single person during her reign — which empress?
Elizabeth of Russia was Empress of Russia (1741–1762). During her reign Elizabeth continued the policies of her father and brought about a remarkable Age of Enlightenment in Russia.
The CEO of the ACS engineering group, this Spanish businessman is better known as the football boss who launched the 'Galácticos' policy of signing the world's best players — who is he?
Florentino Pérez (Spanish; born 8 March 1947) is a Spanish businessman and the president of football club Real Madrid, as well as chairman and CEO of ACS Group, a civil engineering company.
This Roman general and politician, adopted by his uncle Tiberius in AD 4, is best remembered for his campaigns against the German chieftain Arminius. Who was he?
Germanicus (24 May 15 BC - 10 October AD 19) was a Roman general and politician most famously known for his campaigns against Arminius in Germania.
Ascending the throne in 2020 after his cousin's death, this monarch became the fifteenth ruler of a dynasty that has led Oman since the 18th century — who is he?
Haitham bin Tariq (born 11 October 1955) is the Sultan and Prime Minister of Oman.

In the Book of Genesis, this son of Noah appears in the story of Noah's drunkenness and is later named ancestor of the peoples of the Aegean, Anatolia, and Greece — who is he?
Japheth was one of the three sons of Noah in the Book of Genesis.
This U.S. president assumed office in 1841 after his predecessor died just 31 days into his term, becoming the first vice president ever to ascend to the presidency this way — who is he?
John Tyler (March 29, 1790 - January 18, 1862) was the tenth president of the United States, serving from 1841 to 1845, after briefly holding office as the tenth vice president in 1841.
A former Director of Public Prosecutions, this Labour leader became the UK's Prime Minister in 2024 — who is he?
Keir Starmer (born 2 September 1962) is a British politician and former lawyer who has served as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom since 2024 and as Leader of the Labour Party since 2020.
In Christian eschatology, this future event will see Jesus Christ return to sit on a "great white throne" and render a final verdict on every person who has ever lived — what is this event called?
Last Judgment is a central Christian eschatological event marking the return of Jesus Christ to evaluate all of humanity, both the living and the resurrected dead (Jn 5:28-29).

He fought in the Burma Campaign for the British Indian Army and retired a Pakistani colonel, then in 1971 became commander-in-chief and founder of a brand-new nation's armed forces — which four-star general was he?
M. A. G. Osmani (1 September 1918 - 16 February 1984) was a Bangladeshi military officer, revolutionary and politician.
Developed in the Soviet Union by Joseph Stalin, this communist ideology became the predominant state ideology across the Eastern Bloc during the Cold War. What is it?
Marxism–Leninism is a communist ideology that became the largest faction of the communist movement following the October Revolution.
Twice shot in the head and surviving both times, this Russian field marshal later defeated Napoleon's invasion using a strategy of attrition — who was he?
Mikhail Kutuzov was Field Marshal of the Russian Empire (1745–1813).
France's longest-serving head of state across 22 years, he was the country's second president and its very last monarch, deposed in 1870 — who was he?
Napoleon III (born Charles-Louis Napolon Bonaparte; 20 April 1808 - 9 January 1873) was President of France from 1848 to 1852 and then Emperor of the French from 1852 until his deposition in 1870.
Often shown as a nude woman covered in stars and arching protectively over the Earth, this Egyptian deity embodies the sky itself — who is she?
Nut (goddess) (Ancient), also known by various other transcriptions, is the goddess of the sky, stars, cosmos, mothers, astronomy, and the universe in the ancient Egyptian religion.
He started out as a care officer for Camden Council before his drag character Lily Savage made him a household name on British television — which performer was he?
Paul O'Grady (14 June 1955 - 28 March 2023) was an English drag queen, comedian, broadcaster, actor, and writer.
Established by Hitler on 16 March 1939, the day after German troops occupied the Czech rump state, this partially annexed Nazi territory was home mostly to ethnic Czechs — what was it called?
Protectorate of Bohemia and Moravia was a partially annexed territory of Nazi Germany that was established on 16 March 1939 after the German occupation of the Czech lands.
Founder of the System Capital Management investment group, this billionaire is both Ukraine's richest man and the owner of football club Shakhtar Donetsk — who is he?
Rinat Akhmetov (born 21 September 1966) is a Ukrainian oligarch, billionaire and businessman.

A hero of the Texas Revolution, this statesman served as both the first and third president of the Republic of Texas, and is the only American ever elected governor of two different states. Who was he?
Sam Houston (March 2, 1793 - July 26, 1863) was an American military general and statesman who played a prominent role in the Texas Revolution.
This Indian politician has served two separate terms as Chief Minister of Karnataka, and was only the second person ever to complete a full five-year term in that office — who is he?

Siddaramaiah (born 3 August 1947), also referred to by his nickname Siddu, is an Indian politician, lawyer, former lecturer and statesman who served as the 16th Chief Minister of Karnataka from 2013 to 2018 and 2023 to 2026.
Before becoming French prime minister in 2025, this Renaissance party politician held ministerial posts covering local authorities, overseas territories, and the armed forces — who is he?
Sébastien Lecornu (French; born 11 June 1986) is a French politician who has served as Prime Minister of France since September 2025.

Recognized only by the Soviet Union and Mongolia, this partially-recognized socialist state in North Asia existed for 23 years before its parliament requested absorption into the Russian SFSR in 1944 — what was it, whose territory now forms a namesake region of Russia?
Tuvan People's Republic (TPR), known simply as Tuva, was a partially recognized socialist republic that existed between 1921 and 1944 in North Asia.

Walter Model (24 January 1891 - 21 April 1945) was a German Generalfeldmarschall during World War II.

YMCA is a worldwide youth organization based in Vernier, Canton of Geneva, Switzerland, with more than 64 million beneficiaries in 120 countries.
A grandson of caliph Abu Bakr and the first child born to Islam's earliest converts, he led a rival caliphate based in Mecca during the Second Fitna until his death in 692 — who was he?
Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr: Arab leader of Mecca-based caliphate from 683 to 692.

The American spaceflight that first landed humans on the Moon flew in July of which year?
Apollo 11 (July 16-24, 1969) was the American spaceflight that first landed humans on the Moon, and the fifth crewed mission of NASA's Apollo program.
The fifth IOC president and its only American leader, this fierce champion of amateurism is forever linked to the two Olympics he oversaw in Germany, in 1936 and 1972. Who was he?
Avery Brundage: President of the IOC from 1952 to 1972.

Battle of the Yarmuk: 636 CE conflict between the Rashidun Caliphate and Byzantine Empire.
Before becoming Australia's 23rd prime minister, this Rhodes Scholar led the Australian Council of Trade Unions — who was he?
Bob Hawke: Prime Minister of Australia from 1983 to 1991.

Cao Wei: Chinese state (220–266) during the Three Kingdoms period.

Charles Taylor (Liberian politician): President of Liberia from 1997 to 2003.

Cnut: King of Denmark, Norway and England (c.995–1035)

Dhikr: Remembrance of God in Islam.

Fahda bint Falah Al Hithlain: Third wife of King Salman of Saudi Arabia.

Franciscans: Group of religious orders within the Catholic Church connected with St. Francis of Assisi.

Göktürks: Turkic people in Inner Asia.

Hayato Ikeda: Prime Minister of Japan from 1960 to 1964.

Hinduism: Range of Indian religious traditions. Vaidika Dharma (lit. 'Vedic dharma') and Arya Dharma are historical endonyms for Hinduism.

Hungarian People's Republic: Country in Central Europe (1949–1989)

Isaac Herzog: President of Israel since 2021.

Jezebel: Biblical figure; Phoenician princess and wife of Ahab.

Kais Saied: President of Tunisia since 2019. As president, Saied has overseen democratic backsliding, as he has repressed the political opposition and dissidents in Tunisia.
On May 2, 2011, SEAL Team Six carried out Operation Neptune Spear at a compound in Abbottabad, Pakistan, ending a manhunt that began with the war in Afghanistan — what event was this?
Killing of Osama bin Laden: 2011 U.S. military operation in Abbottabad, Pakistan.
In Arthurian legend, this enchantress figure gifts Excalibur to the king, raises the knight Lancelot, and later helps carry the dying king to Avalon — who or what is she?
Lady of the Lake: Sorceress in Arthurian legend. As either single character or multiple ones, the figure of the Lady of the Lake often appears in various roles in the works of modern culture.

Shaped by liberal ideas and the non-aggression principle, this political philosophy prizes liberty and personal sovereignty above all, holding you may live as you choose so long as you don't force or defraud others — what is it?
Libertarianism: Political philosophy based on liberty. Different categorizations have been used to distinguish these various forms of libertarianism.
A wealthy merchant who bribed his way into making a hostage prince the heir to the Qin throne, this chancellor later served as regent for the boy who became China's First Emperor — who is he?

Pompey: Roman general and statesman (106–48 BC)

Republic of Artsakh: Breakaway state in the South Caucasus (1991–2023). The conflict erupted into a full-out war in 1992.

A vocal critic of the Federal Reserve and mass surveillance programs, this Texas congressman ran for president as the Libertarian nominee in 1988 before seeking the Republican nomination twice more — who is he?

This French Romantic giant gave the world both 'The Hunchback of Notre-Dame' and a sprawling 1862 novel that became a beloved musical — who was he?

War in Iraq (2013–2017): Armed Conflict in the Middle East.

What is the atomic number of Chlorine?
Chlorine is a chemical element; it has symbol Cl and atomic number 17.
In what year was Marie Curie born?
Marie Curie: Curie was born in Warsaw, Russian Empire, where she studied at the clandestine Flying University and began her practical scientific training.
In what year was Nitroglycerin discovered?
Nitroglycerin: It is combined with nitrocellulose to form double-based smokeless powder, used as a propellant in artillery and firearms since the 1880s.
In what year was Thallium discovered?
Thallium is a chemical element; it has symbol Tl and atomic number 81.
Ceftriaxone: Pfizer. Ceftriaxone, sold under the brand name Rocephin, is a third-generation cephalosporin antibiotic used for the treatment of a number of bacterial infections.
In which country is Convair B-58 Hustler based?
Convair B-58 Hustler: United States. The Convair B-58 Hustler is a supersonic strategic bomber, the first capable of Mach 2 flight.
Who is credited with discovering Dubnium?
Dubnium: Joint Institute for Nuclear Research. Dubnium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Db and atomic number 105.
Who is credited with discovering Brainfuck?
Brainfuck: Urban Müller. Brainfuck is an esoteric programming language created in 1993 by Swiss student Urban Müller.
Who is credited with discovering Cobalt?
Cobalt: Georg Brandt. Cobalt is a chemical element; it has symbol Co and atomic number 27.
Home to both edible and poisonous species, this fungal genus supplies the West's most popular cultivated mushrooms, including the everyday button mushroom — which genus is it?
Agaricus is a genus of mushroom-forming fungi containing both edible and poisonous species, with over 400 members worldwide and possibly again as many disputed or newly discovered species.
Found on every continent but Antarctica and almost always monogamous breeders, which bird family unites ducks, geese, and swans under one scientific name?
Anatidae are the biological family of water birds that includes ducks, geese, and swans.
Native to Europe and Asia, which genus of burdock plants owes its seed-dispersal success to burrs that later inspired a famous fastening invention?
Arctium is a genus of biennial plants commonly known as burdock, family Asteraceae.
Created in 1989 by Brian Fox for the GNU Project as a free replacement for the Bourne shell, this command-line interpreter became the default login shell on countless Linux systems — which shell?
Bash (Unix shell) (short for "Bourne Again SHell") is an interactive command interpreter and command language developed for Unix-like operating systems.
Native to India and Nepal, this medium-sized antelope sports a striking two-tone coat, with males growing corkscrew horns up to 75 cm long. Which animal is it?
Blackbuck (Antilope cervicapra), also known as the Indian antelope, is a medium-sized antelope native to India and Nepal.
This small leafy vegetable, a cultivar of cabbage grown for its edible buds, shares its name with a European capital — what is it?
Brussels sprout is a member of the Gemmifera cultivar group of cabbages (Brassica oleracea), grown for its edible buds.

This American astronomer and planetary scientist was initially an assistant professor at Harvard before moving to Cornell as the David Duncan Professor of Astronomy. He played an active role in the Voyager programs. Who is he?
Carl Sagan (November 9, 1934 - December 20, 1996) was an American astronomer, planetary scientist and science communicator.
Patented in 1948 and used to treat hay fever and other allergic conditions, this first-generation antihistamine works within two hours by blocking the H1 histamine receptor — name the drug?
Chlorphenamine (CP, CPM), also known as chlorpheniramine, is an antihistamine used to treat the symptoms of allergic conditions such as allergic rhinitis (hay fever).

This highly venomous, nocturnal snake, black or bluish-black with narrow white crossbands, is widely distributed across South Asia, from grasslands to agricultural fields to human settlements — what snake is it?
Common krait (Bungarus caeruleus) is a highly venomous snake species belonging to the genus Bungarus in the family Elapidae.
Its name comes from the Greek for "dark blue," and its anion — a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen — is so toxic that salts like the sodium and potassium forms cause swift poisoning. What is it?
Cyanide (from Greek kyanos 'dark blue') is an inorganic chemical compound that contains a CN functional group.
This Russian chemist's great law let him predict three undiscovered elements — germanium, gallium, and scandium — and a synthetic element now bears his name; who was he?
This Russian economist served as Vladimir Putin's economic adviser before becoming governor of her country's central bank, and was ranked among Forbes' most powerful women in 2019 — who is she?
Elvira Nabiullina (born 29 October 1963) is a Russian economist and current governor of the Central Bank of Russia.
This sensory organ detects light and converts it into electro-chemical signals in neurons, using an adjustable lens system to focus incoming light and form images — name the organ?
Eye is a sensory organ that allows an organism to perceive visual information.
He worked on uranium enrichment during the Manhattan Project, then — after McCarthyism cost him his physics post — founded San Francisco's hands-on Exploratorium museum; who was he?

Frank Oppenheimer (August 14, 1912 - February 3, 1985) was an American particle physicist, cattle rancher, professor of physics at the University of Colorado, and the founder of the Exploratorium in San Francisco.
The largest and outermost of the three hip muscles, this one shapes the buttocks and helps keep the human trunk upright — what muscle is it?
Gluteus maximus is the main extensor muscle of the hip in humans.
Though usually grouped with the birch family, some botanists split this deciduous shrub genus into its own family — and its nut is a popular snack — which plant?
Hazel are plants of the genus Corylus of deciduous trees and large shrubs native to the temperate Northern Hemisphere.
Named for a Greek youth beloved by Apollo and slain by a jealous wind god who then transformed him into this fragrant spring bloom — what flower genus is it?
Hyacinth is a genus of bulbous herbs and spring-blooming perennials.
Resembling a lump of burnt charcoal growing on birch bark, this parasitic fungus is popularly called chaga — what's its scientific name?
Inonotus obliquus (a Latinization of the Russian word), is a fungus in the family Hymenochaetaceae.
Holder of 128 firearm patents, this American engineer invented the telescoping bolt that made compact autoloading pistols possible — who is he?

John Browning (January 23, 1855 - November 26, 1926) was an American firearm designer who developed many varieties of military and civilian firearms, cartridges, and gun mechanisms, many of which are still in use around the world.
Despite its name suggesting a root vegetable, this biennial cultivar of wild cabbage grows a swollen edible stem above ground and is related to broccoli, kale, and Brussels sprouts — what is it?
Kohlrabi (scientific name Brassica oleracea Gongylodes Group), also called German turnip or turnip cabbage, is a biennial vegetable, a low, stout cultivar of wild cabbage.

Named after the Italian word for lemon, this colorless liquid hydrocarbon is the main compound behind citrus peel fragrance, occurring mostly as a right-handed form extracted commercially by centrifugal separation or steam distillation - name the compound?

Limonene is a colorless liquid aliphatic hydrocarbon classified as a cyclic monoterpene, and is the major component in the fragrance and essential oil of citrus fruit peels, taking its name from Italian limone ("lemon").
This marsupial family native to Australia and New Guinea includes kangaroos, wallabies, quokkas, and tree-kangaroos among its 63 living species — what family is it?
Macropodidae is a family of marsupials that includes kangaroos, wallabies, tree-kangaroos, wallaroos, pademelons, the quokka, and several other groups.
This nitrogen-heavy compound forms durable plastic resins used in dry-erase boards and dinnerware, and its foam version scrubs stains as the innards of a Magic Eraser — name the chemical?
Melamine is an organic compound with the formula C3H6N6.
This SI base unit for amount of substance, symbol mol, is defined so that one unit contains exactly 6.02214076×10²³ elementary entities — what is it called?
Mole (unit) (symbol mol) is a unit of measurement, the base unit in the International System of Units (SI) for amount of substance.

The first recognized fossil of this archaic human group was unearthed in 1856 in a German valley, and the species vanished around 40,000 years ago as modern humans arrived; who were these Pleistocene Europeans?

Neanderthal (nee-(r)-TAHL, nay-, -THAHL; Homo neanderthalensis or sometimes Homo sapiens neanderthalensis) are an extinct group of archaic humans who inhabited Europe and Western and Central Asia during the Middle to Late Pleistocene.

Synthesized in 2002 at a lab near Moscow and named in 2016 for the physicist who hunted down the heaviest atoms, this synthetic element claims the highest atomic number and atomic mass of anything yet known — which is it?
Oganesson is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Og and atomic number 118.
Found in organs such as the brain and lungs, inside flatworms, and within leaf cross-sections, this word names an organism's bulk functional tissue — what is it?
Parenchyma is the bulk of functional substance in an animal organ such as the brain or lungs, or a structure such as a tumour.
Made in the body from the amino acid L-phenylalanine, this natural stimulant also turns up in fermented chocolate and inhibits a transporter called VMAT2 — what is it?
Phenethylamine (PEA) is an organic compound, natural monoamine alkaloid, and trace amine, which acts as a central nervous system stimulant in humans.
It looks like a single point of light, but this brightest star of Ursa Minor is actually a triple star system parked near the north celestial pole — what is it?
Polaris is a yellow supergiant star in the northern circumpolar constellation of Ursa Minor.
This noncontagious autoimmune condition leaves dry, scaly patches of skin and can flare at the exact spot of an injury — a quirk called the Koebner phenomenon; what is it?
Psoriasis is a long-lasting, noncontagious autoimmune disease characterized by patches of abnormal skin.

This condition, often triggered by crush injuries or extreme exercise, causes skeletal muscle to break down so rapidly that it can turn urine tea-colored and damage the kidneys — what condition is it?
Rhabdomyolysis (shortened as rhabdo) is a condition in which damaged skeletal muscle breaks down rapidly.
Contracted from contaminated food, this bacterial illness typically causes diarrhea, fever, and cramps within a day or two of exposure — what is it called?
Salmonellosis is a symptomatic infection caused by bacteria of the genus Salmonella.
Cartilaginous and toothy, these fish are the sister group to the rays and skates and trace their ancestors to the Devonian Period — what are they?

Shark are a group of elasmobranch cartilaginous fishes characterized by a ribless endoskeleton, dermal denticles, five to seven gill slits on each side, and pectoral fins that are not fused to the head.
This leafy green vegetable's high oxalate content gives raw and cooked versions noticeably different flavors, with blanching helping to tone it down — what vegetable is it?
Spinach (Spinacia oleracea) is a leafy green flowering plant native to Central and Western Asia.
This South African biologist established the tiny roundworm C. elegans as a model organism, work that helped earn him a share of the 2002 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Who was he?
Sydney Brenner (13 January 1927 - 5 April 2019) was a South African biologist.

Beloved by biologists for its wild morphological variation and elaborate nest-building, this northern fish tolerates big swings in salinity, living in the sea but breeding in fresh water — what is it?
Three-spined stickleback (Gasterosteus aculeatus) is a fish native to most inland and coastal waters north of 30N.
These large, heavyset American game birds have a distinctive fleshy growth called a snood hanging from the base of their beak, with wild and ocellated species. What birds are they?
Turkey (bird) are large, heavyset galliforms in the genus Meleagris, indigenous to the Americas.
This pungent Japanese condiment, ground from the rhizome of a plant related to horseradish and mustard, traditionally accompanies sushi. What is it?

This teenage prodigy's work on solvable polynomials helped birth what's now called group theory, and his fiery Republican politics landed him in prison before a fatal duel ended his life at 20 — who was he?
Évariste Galois (25 October 1811 - 31 May 1832) was a French mathematician and political activist.
This practice leans on 'branding' — tying a name or image to certain qualities in people's minds — to nudge them toward buying more. What field is it?
Advertising: Form of communication for marketing.
This German polar researcher proposed in 1912 that the continents were slowly drifting apart, a theory mainstream geology only accepted decades later thanks to palaeomagnetism — who was he?
Alfred Wegener: German climatologist and geophysicist (1880–1930)
Critically endangered with barely two dozen wild individuals estimated in 2007, this big cat subspecies survives along the Russian-Chinese border in the Primorye region — which spotted predator?
Amur leopard: Subspecies of large cat. The Amur leopard (Panthera pardus orientalis) is a leopard subspecies native to the Primorye region of southeastern Russia and northern China.
This external body opening at the end of the digestive tract, positioned opposite the mouth, lets gas and solid waste pass out after digestion?
Anus: Digestive tract waste expulsion opening. Passage of feces through the anus is typically controlled by muscular sphincters, and failure to stop unwanted passages results in fecal incontinence.
Native to Eurasia, this perennial plant is grown as a vegetable crop for its tender young shoots, harvested in the spring — what's this vegetable?
Asparagus: Species of flowering plant in the family Asparagaceae.
A Kenyan economist who met his future wife at the University of Hawaii, this man became the father of a future U.S. president and the subject of that son's 1995 memoir — who is he?
Before becoming TV's most famous bow-tied science educator, this Boeing mechanical engineer invented a hydraulic resonance suppressor tube for 747s, then quit to do sketch comedy. Who is he?

A twin-engine, carrier-capable strike fighter flown by the U.S., Australia, and Kuwait, this larger, more advanced follow-on to an earlier 1980s Navy jet packs an internal 20 mm rotary cannon and can be rigged as an airborne refueling tanker — what is it called?
The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom
Boeing F/A-18E/F Super Hornet: Series of carrier-based multirole combat aircraft.
Despite the name, this pseudocereal isn't related to true cereals at all — it's kin to rhubarb and sorrel, and was first cultivated in Yunnan around 6,000 BC — which crop is it?
Buckwheat: Species of flowering plant in the family Polygonaceae.
This suborder of 'dog-like' carnivores includes bears, raccoons, weasels, and seals, and is thought to have diversified mainly across North America and northern Eurasia — what's it called?
Caniformia: Suborder of mammals. Caniformia is a suborder within the order Carnivora consisting of "dog-like" carnivorans.
Named for barbels that resemble a cat's whiskers, these scaleless, ray-finned fish include giants like the Mekong species and go by nicknames such as 'mud cat' in the Southern US — what are they?
Catfish: Order of fish. Catfish are a diverse group of ray-finned fish of the order Siluriformes (historically Nematognathi).
Domesticated from the red junglefowl roughly 8,000 years ago, this bird now numbers over 26 billion worldwide, more than any other domesticated species — what is it?
Chicken: Domesticated subspecies of red junglefowl. The chicken (Gallus gallus domesticus) is the domesticated form of the red junglefowl (Gallus gallus), originally native to Southeast Asia.
Sold under the brand name Anafranil, this tricyclic antidepressant treats obsessive-compulsive disorder but also premature ejaculation and the cataplexy that comes with narcolepsy — which drug?
Clomipramine: Antidepressant. It has also been notably used to treat premature ejaculation and the cataplexy associated with narcolepsy.
The heaviest songbird on Earth and the most widely distributed of all the corvids, this all-black passerine averages 25 inches long across the Northern Hemisphere — what is it?
Common raven: Large, black species of passerine bird.

This academic framework examines how systemic bias against certain ethnic groups is embedded in laws and institutions, using the concept of intersectionality to explain overlapping forms of inequality — what is it called?
Critical race theory: Conceptual framework. The word critical in the name is an academic reference to critical theory, not criticizing or blaming individuals.

Dubbed the 'father of modern experimental optics,' this Scottish inventor discovered the angle and the photoelasticity that bear on polarized light — and improved the stereoscope along the way. Who was he?
David Brewster: British astronomer and mathematician (1781–1868)
Sold as Benadryl, this first-generation H1-antihistamine is famously sedating — yet at higher doses it can paradoxically cause agitation and restlessness instead of sleep; what's the drug?
Diphenhydramine: Antihistamine medication. Diphenhydramine, sold under the brand name Benadryl among others, is an antihistamine and sedative.
Known medically as cerumen, this waxy secretion in the ear canal protects against bacteria, fungi, and water while trapping dust and dead skin — what is it?
Earwax: Waxy substance secreted by the ear.

Distinguished by its massive head, huge size, and trademark black facial mask, this gentle British dog breed is now classed as vulnerable in its homeland, with just 104 UK births recorded in 2020 — which breed?
English Mastiff: British breed of dog. The English Mastiff, or simply the Mastiff, is a British breed of very large dog of mastiff type.
This small European finch's male sports a blue-grey cap and rust-red underparts, while both sexes flash white wing bars — what species is it?
Eurasian chaffinch: Species of bird. The Eurasian chaffinch, common chaffinch, or simply the chaffinch (Fringilla coelebs) is a common and widespread small passerine bird – in the finch family.
A feathery, yellow-flowered Mediterranean herb in the carrot family, this anise-tasting plant is one of the primary ingredients in absinthe — what is it?
Fennel: Flowering plant species in the carrot family.
Named for the mathematician who used it to solve the heat equation, this expansion writes a periodic function as an infinite sum of sines and cosines — what is it?
Fourier series: Decomposition of periodic functions.
Commonly known as snails and slugs, this class is the second-largest in the animal kingdom after insects — what is it called?
Gastropod: Class of molluscs. The fossil record of gastropods extends back to the Late Cambrian.
Occurring in the cytosol, this ten-step metabolic pathway breaks glucose down into pyruvate while generating ATP and NADH — what process is it?
Glycolysis: Series of interconnected biochemical reactions.

Once nearly all lumped into a single genus before 21st-century research proved that grouping polyphyletic, these grey-and-white seabirds have an older dialect name, 'mew,' echoing their calls — which birds?
Gull: Subfamily of seabirds. The large species take up to four years to attain full adult plumage, but two years is typical for small gulls.
Comprising cicadas, aphids, bed bugs, and more than 80,000 other species with piercing-sucking mouthparts, which insect order is nicknamed the 'true bugs'?
Hemiptera: Order of insects often called true bugs.
Often called the founder of alpinism and modern meteorology, this Genevan scientist is also credited with building the first successful solar oven — who was he?
Horace Bénédict de Saussure: Genevan scientist and mountaineer (1740–1799)
Marked in its severe stage by hallucinations and paradoxical undressing, which condition is defined as a body core temperature below 35 degrees Celsius?
Hypothermia: Human body core temperature below 35 °C (95 °F)
This ring-shaped structure in the eye controls how much light reaches the retina by adjusting the size of the pupil — and it's also what determines eye color — what is it?
Iris (anatomy): Colored part of an eye.
This businessman and chemist owned the Lakers through their 1980s 'Showtime' era, winning 10 NBA titles before a Hall of Fame induction as a contributor — who was he?
Jerry Buss: American businessman and investor (1933–2013)
Sometimes grown just for looks, this cabbage relative's leaves can be bumpy, curly, or flat, in colors from purple to green — what leafy vegetable is it?
Kale: Form of cabbage with green or purple leaves.
This is the most abundant genus of trees on Earth, dominating the boreal forests of Siberia and Canada despite dropping its needles every fall. What genus is it?
Larch: Genus of deciduous conifers in the family Pinaceae.
Syntax, semantics, morphology, phonetics, phonology, and pragmatics are all branches of which scientific field?
This American experimental physicist won the 1968 Nobel Prize for discovering resonance states using the hydrogen bubble chamber — who was he?
Luis Walter Alvarez: American physicist, inventor and professor (1911–1988)
Native to the Malay Peninsula and Borneo, this tropical fruit hides sweet, tangy white flesh beneath a deep reddish-purple rind — which fruit?
Mangosteen: Tropical evergreen tree with edible fruit.
Combined with formaldehyde to create hardwearing resins found in Formica countertops, plastic dinnerware, and the foam in a Magic Eraser, this nitrogen-rich compound also resists fire — what is it?
Melamine: Fire-resistant chemical used in dinnerware, insulation, and cleaning products.
Often striking one side of the head and sometimes preceded by a sensory 'aura,' this neurological disorder brings nausea and sensitivity to light and sound — what is it?
Migraine: Disorder resulting in recurrent moderate–severe headaches.
Sold under the brand name Singulair, this asthma medication blocks leukotriene D4 in the lungs but received a UK black box warning in 2019 over neuropsychiatric side effects — what is it?
Montelukast: Medication used in asthma or COPD.
Nicknamed the 'brain-eating amoeba,' this free-living microorganism lurks in warm freshwater lakes, hot springs, and poorly chlorinated pools — what is it?

Named for a mythological daughter of Tantalus, this silvery transition metal with atomic number 41 was once called columbium and is now prized as a nickel-free option in hypoallergenic jewelry — which element?
Niobium: Chemical element with atomic number 41 (Nb)
Born in Nishapur during the Seljuk era, this Persian polymath solved general cubic equations using intersecting conic sections centuries before Descartes — who was he?
Omar Khayyam: Persian polymath and poet (1048–1131)
A perennial herb from the mountains of East Asia, its root is the original source of a famous herbal supplement — though studies find little evidence it actually works. Which plant?
Panax ginseng: Species of flowering plant.
Almost every member of this flightless, countershaded clan sticks to the Southern Hemisphere — except one lone species that creeps up to the equator in the Galapagos. What bird is it?
Penguin: Family of aquatic flightless birds.
Plants, algae, and cyanobacteria run this light-powered process, splitting water to release oxygen as a byproduct while banking energy in sugars like glucose. What is it called?
Photosynthesis: Biological process to convert light into chemical energy.
Whether natural silk or synthetic nylon, this class of polymer is defined by repeating units joined through amide bonds — what is it?
Polyamide: Macromolecule with repeating units linked by amide bonds.
Genetic studies trace this most widely cultivated apricot species to Central Asia, though its scientific name nods to a country in the Caucasus — what is it?
Prunus armeniaca: Species of apricot. The native range is somewhat uncertain due to its extensive prehistoric cultivation.
About the size of a house cat, this nocturnal herbivorous marsupial thrives on Rottnest Island near Perth and is the only member of its genus — what is it?
Quokka: Small marsupial from southwestern Australia.

Covering more than 200 conditions from arthritis to soft-tissue pain syndromes, this umbrella term for chronic joint and connective-tissue pain gives its name to a whole medical specialty — what is it called?
Rheumatism: Medical conditions affecting the joints or connective tissue.
Known as rue or 'herb-of-grace,' this Mediterranean plant is prized for its bluish leaves and doubles as an insect repellent — which species?
Ruta graveolens: Species of plant. Ruta graveolens, commonly known as rue, common rue, ruda, arruda or herb-of-grace, is a species of the genus Ruta grown as an ornamental plant and herb.
This genus contains most of the world's familiar bushy-tailed tree squirrels, found across North America, Europe, temperate Asia, and Central and South America — which genus?
This Japanese army medical officer led a biological and chemical warfare unit in Japanese-occupied Manchuria during World War II and was later granted immunity — who is he?
Shirō Ishii: Japanese biological weapons specialist (1892–1959)
Famous for a repetitive, melodic call often referenced in poetry, this brown, spotted-breasted bird uses a favorite stone as an 'anvil' to crack open snail shells — which species?
Song thrush: Species of bird. The song thrush (Turdus philomelos) is a thrush that breeds across the West Palearctic.
This retired American physician turned ufologist founded both a center for extraterrestrial-intelligence study and a project pushing for the release of classified UFO information — who is he?
This Polish tax advisor turned politician placed third in the 2025 presidential election while chairing the libertarian New Hope party — who is he?
Sławomir Mentzen: Polish economist and politician (born 1986)
This large mass of gray matter sits between the cerebral cortex and the midbrain, relaying sensory and motor signals to the cortex while regulating sleep and alertness — what is this brain structure?
Thalamus: Structure within the brain. It has several functions, such as the relaying of sensory and motor signals to the cerebral cortex and the regulation of consciousness, sleep, and alertness.
Also known as the Mexican husk tomato, this nightshade fruit has been cultivated since pre-Columbian times and is the key ingredient in salsa verde — what is it?

This large flatfish native to the Northeast Atlantic, Baltic, and Mediterranean gave its name to a 1990s fishing dispute between Canada and Spain, even though a different species was the real catch at stake — which fish?
Turbot: Species of flatfish in the family Scophthalmidae.
Born in 1946, this German facilitator and non-fiction writer built a career exploring esoteric subjects until her death in 2011 — who was she?
Vera F. Birkenbihl: German facilitator, writer. Vera Felicitas Birkenbihl (26 April 1946 - 3 December 2011) was a German facilitator, non-fiction writer, and esoteric.
First isolated in 1669 by alchemist Henning Brand, this waxy, translucent form of an element glows faintly green in the dark and ignites spontaneously in air — which substance?
Sold under the brand name Ambien, which nonbenzodiazepine 'Z-drug' cuts the time to fall asleep by about fifteen minutes?
